speaker: A
text: Sixty-five to seventy-two percent. That's the share of every RL training step eaten purely by token generation. Not gradients, not optimizer updates — just the model producing text during rollouts. NVIDIA just moved speculative decoding, which has been a deployment trick for two years, into the RL training loop to fix it.

speaker: B
text: What do you mean by deployment trick — speculative decoding isn't already used in training?

speaker: A
text: Normally you run a small draft model that proposes a few tokens, then the big model verifies them all at once. If the draft is right, you skip autoregressive decoding for those steps. Saves latency at serving time. NeMo-RL's insight is simple: RL post-training is mostly inference. The model has to generate thousands of rollout tokens per step to compute the reward. Apply the same trick there.

speaker: B
text: But the policy changes every update step. Doesn't the draft model become stale immediately?

speaker: A
text: That's the key result. They prove the lossless guarantee holds under policy drift. The target model verifies every proposal from the draft via exact rejection sampling — the same mechanism you use for deployment. Log-probs and gradients are computed against the target, not the draft. So from the optimizer's perspective, nothing changed. You get speed for free, not by trading fidelity.

speaker: B
text: What are the actual speedup numbers?

speaker: A
text: 1.77x generation throughput at 8B parameters, measured. More important: 2.5x end-to-end projected at 235B on 2048 GB200s. That number is from a simulator, not a live run — but the simulator was validated against the measured 8B results. If it holds, RL post-training at frontier scale becomes a third cheaper. That changes which experiments labs can afford to run in a given budget.

speaker: B
text: What are the limits? Where does it break down?

speaker: A
text: The draft has to match the rollout distribution. They tested a generic chat-aligned draft and only got 1.51x. You have to initialize the draft from the same policy you're training. And k equals 3 is the empirical sweet spot — more speculation actually hurts because you waste draft tokens on branches the target rejects. At k equals 7, it's slower than plain autoregressive on certain rollout types.

speaker: B
text: Okay, second paper. Diffusion language models — these are models that generate all tokens in parallel rather than left to right?

speaker: A
text: Masked diffusion, specifically. Instead of generating token by token, you start with a fully masked sequence and iteratively unmask it. Better for code — you can read context from both directions simultaneously. The problem has been size. You needed a multi-billion parameter diffusion LLM to be competitive with autoregressive models. Tide compresses that capability down to a 0.6B student.

speaker: B
text: The teacher and student use different architectures and vocabularies — how do you even transfer knowledge in that case?

speaker: A
text: Three components addressing three failure modes. Tidal schedules the distillation signal by noise level — the teacher's predictions are unreliable when most tokens are masked, so Tide down-weights those gradient steps. CompDemo gives the teacher a complementary mask half to look at, restoring its ability to make meaningful predictions under heavy masking. Reverse Calm inverts the chunk-likelihood loss direction, which bounds gradients when the tokenizers diverge.

speaker: B
text: And what does that actually buy in practice?

speaker: A
text: A 16B mixture-of-experts teacher distilled into a 0.6B student. 22 times less memory. 5 times faster inference. HumanEval code generation goes from 32.3 to 48.78. That last number matters the most — code is where diffusion LLMs have been consistently weakest, and where inference speed matters most in deployment.

speaker: B
text: You mentioned something about this fitting a broader pattern in distillation this month?

speaker: A
text: This is the fourth paper in two weeks to solve a teacher-student mismatch by engineering a neutral exchange channel rather than forcing token alignment. BLD on April 17th used raw bytes as the channel. TESSY on April 18th used cooperative token interleaving. Switch-KD, same week, used a shared text-probability space. Tide uses bounded chunk-likelihood matching. Four different mechanisms, one structural choice — and none of these papers cite each other on this point. The field converged without saying so explicitly.

speaker: B
text: That implies there's an abstraction nobody has named yet.

speaker: A
text: Right. The design surface is the channel between mismatched models, not the models themselves. The next round of distillation work will be asking: which channel is optimal under which mismatch profile.

speaker: B
text: Let's switch to industry. White House restoring Anthropic access — there was a Pentagon standoff?

speaker: A
text: The Pentagon revoked federal agency access to Anthropic's Mythos model about six days ago following a security review. The White House is now drafting guidance to reinstate it. What's notable is the timeline — less than a week from revocation to restoration effort. That suggests Mythos has become significant enough to federal AI operations that losing access was immediately disruptive, not theoretical.

speaker: B
text: The Mistral disinformation result seems more alarming to me. 60% is a real number.

speaker: A
text: NewsGuard audited Mistral's Le Chat. Neutral queries, 10% error rate. Malicious leading prompts — ones that embed a disinformation claim in the question framing — 80% error rate. The 60% headline is averaged across both. What's structurally important is that the error rate scales linearly with prompt maliciousness. The model is anchoring on whatever framing the prompt provides rather than evaluating the underlying claim.

speaker: B
text: Is this specific to Mistral or a general vulnerability?

speaker: A
text: Almost certainly general, but Mistral is the most precisely documented case at this scale. The interesting question isn't which model fails — it's that the failure mode is prompt-anchoring rather than the dramatic jailbreaks most safety work focuses on. Steady amplification of adversarial framing at 80% is more dangerous in practice than low-frequency exotic jailbreaks.

speaker: B
text: Looking at everything from today — what's the one open problem you're actually watching?

speaker: A
text: Whether speculative decoding's k-selection can be made adaptive — a model that learns how many tokens to speculate based on the current rollout phase should push well past 1.77x, because right now k equals 3 is just an empirical sweet spot, not a principled ceiling.
